tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 87: Cars, Trucks, Auto Parts & Bicycles — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing a Car into the U.S.: EPA 3520-1, DOT HS-7, 25-Year Rule, USMCA U.S. Content & Legal Ways to Lower Auto Tariffs (HTS Ch. 87) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 87 line needs at U.S. entry — EPA Form 3520-1, the DOT HS-7 declaration, registered importers, the 25-year rule, CPSC bicycle rules, AD/CVD — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA U.S. content, vehicle-part status, deal rates, the certified-parts election, drawback and foreign-trade zones.
keywords: importing a car to the us
importing a used car to the us

tariffEngineering.intro:
**Vehicles are regulated products.** A car, truck or motorcycle enters only if it meets the U.S. emission and safety standards or qualifies for an exemption: the importer files **EPA Form 3520-1** (3520-21 for heavy-duty engines) and the **DOT HS-7** declaration with the entry. A vehicle built to U.S. standards carries the manufacturer's EPA label and FMVSS certification label; a non-conforming one must go through an EPA Independent Commercial Importer and a NHTSA Registered Importer, or be at least **25 years old** (NHTSA) — EPA's own age exemption follows its separate rules. ATVs, off-highway motorcycles and snowmobiles follow EPA's nonroad rules; bicycles and low-speed e-bikes the CPSC bicycle standard; wheelchairs are FDA devices.

On cost, the levers are: proving **U.S. content** for USMCA vehicles, claiming **USMCA** on parts, showing whether a listed article is really a **car or truck part**, the right **classification** (a cab chassis pays 4% where a complete truck pays 25%), the **country deal rates**, the opt-in **certified-parts** headings, and the usual **drawback**, **foreign-trade zone**, first-sale and **Chapter 98** provisions.

levers.title: Get Commerce approval of the U.S. content of USMCA vehicles
levers.saves: The 25% Section 232 duty on the U.S.-content share: a $40,000 USMCA SUV with $16,000 of U.S. content pays $6,000 instead of $10,000
levers.appliesTo: Passenger vehicles and light trucks (note 33(b)) and medium- and heavy-duty trucks (note 38(b)) from Mexico or Canada that qualify for USMCA; not buses
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin, plus the Secretary of Commerce's approval of the importer's documentation of U.S. content (parts wholly obtained, produced entirely or substantially transformed in the United States); the entry is split into a 9903.94.03 (or 9903.74.03) line for the non-U.S. content and a 9903.94.02 (or 9903.74.06) line for the U.S. content.
levers.caveat: Without an approval the 25% is charged on the full value. The vehicle must first qualify under the USMCA automotive rules of origin (general note 11). Buses of 8702 pay 10% on the full value.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim USMCA on parts and other goods from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate, the 25% Section 232 parts duty (car and truck parts) and the 10% Section 301 duty: a USMCA axle pays nothing instead of 27.5%
levers.appliesTo: Auto parts of 8706–8708 and the other listed parts, truck parts, motorcycles, bicycles, trailers and other goods from Mexico or Canada
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, with the records showing the good meets the USMCA rule (regional value content and the other automotive requirements for vehicle parts).
levers.caveat: Knock-down kits and parts compilations are not covered by the parts relief. Canada's Section 338 duty (golf carts, small vehicles) applies even to USMCA goods, and USMCA does not lift the Section 232 metals duty on trailers, bumpers and other derivatives.

levers.title: Show whether a listed article is really a car or truck part
levers.saves: The 25% Section 232 parts duty (15% or 10% from deal partners) on listed articles that are not parts of passenger vehicles, light trucks or medium- and heavy-duty vehicles — they pay the base rate plus the Section 301 duty for the country instead
levers.appliesTo: The note 33(g) and 38(i) lines: chassis, bodies, most of 8708 (for example axles, brakes, gearboxes for farm tractors, forklifts or other machinery), trailer parts of 8716.90.50
levers.document: Product specifications and sales records showing the vehicle the article is designed and sold for; enter it under 9903.94.06 (note 33(h)(ii)) or 9903.74.11 (note 38(l)).
levers.caveat: CBP looks at the article as designed and sold; a part sold for both uses is a vehicle part for the share used in cars or trucks. Most of these articles from China still pay the 25% List 3 duty.

citations.label: CBP Section 232 FAQs: automobiles and parts

levers.title: Classify the vehicle by what it is as imported
levers.saves: Up to 25 points of base rate and the Section 232 vehicle duty: a cab chassis (8704.22.11, 4%) vs a complete truck (8704.22.51, 25%); a passenger vehicle (8703, 2.5%) vs a goods vehicle (8704, 25%); a vehicle of 8703.21 (up to 1,000 cc) or 8703.10 outside the auto action
levers.appliesTo: Vans, pickups, cab chassis, side-by-sides and ATVs, golf carts, e-bikes (8711.60, Free) vs bicycles (8712, 11%)
levers.document: A binding ruling from CBP describing the vehicle as imported: design, seating, cargo area, engine, G.V.W., motor power.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the vehicle's condition and principal design at import; post-import conversion does not change it and is examined. Chapter note 3: chassis fitted with cabs go to 8702–8704, not 8706.

levers.title: Know the country of origin and the deal rates
levers.saves: The gap between 15% (EU, Japan, Korea cars and parts; Taiwan parts), 10% (UK cars in quota, UK listed parts) and 27.5% (cars from other countries) — or 127.5% for a Chinese EV
levers.appliesTo: Passenger vehicles, light trucks and listed auto parts
levers.document: Production records showing where the vehicle or part was last substantially transformed, and the origin marking.
levers.caveat: The deal rates are floors: a 25% pickup from Japan, the EU or Korea stays at 25%. UK cars pay 27.5% once the quarterly or annual quota fills. Trucks, buses and truck parts have no deal rates.

levers.title: Use the certified-parts election when it is cheaper
levers.saves: Parts that would pay the 25% metals duty (or 25% + Section 301) can enter at 15% in total from the EU, Japan, Korea or Taiwan, 10% from the UK for UK-built cars, or 25% from elsewhere with no Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: Parts not on the note 33(g) / 38(i) lists and not in chapters 72, 73 or 76 that will be used for U.S. vehicle production or repair — for example other parts of 8708.99 that now pay the metals duty
levers.document: The importer of record's certification that the parts will be used for automobile (or MHDV) production or repair in the United States, with the information CBP requires (headings 9903.94.07, .33, .45, .55, .65, .69; 9903.74.09).
levers.caveat: An election, not a requirement: from countries without a deal it raises the duty on parts that would otherwise pay only the 10%–12.5% Section 301 rate. USMCA parts certified this way pay nothing (9903.94.06, 9903.74.10).

levers.title: Vehicles 25 years old or more
levers.saves: The 25% Section 232 vehicle duty (9903.94.04, 9903.74.07) — a 25-year-old import from Japan pays 12.5% instead of 15%, from a country without a deal its base rate plus Section 301 instead of 27.5%
levers.appliesTo: Passenger vehicles, light trucks and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles manufactured in a year at least 25 years before the year of entry
levers.document: Proof of the manufacture date (title, build plate, VIN decoding); for NHTSA, the HS-7 declaration that the vehicle is 25 or more years old.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duty still applies (note 52(f) does not list 9903.94.04). EPA has its own rules: a vehicle not exempt by age under 40 CFR 85.1511 needs an EPA-compliant entry.

levers.title: Bring back your own vehicle duty-free
levers.saves: All duty on a U.S. resident's vehicle taken abroad and returned, and on U.S.-made goods returned unchanged
levers.appliesTo: Cars, motorcycles, trailers and other vehicles taken abroad by U.S. residents; American-made vehicles and parts returned without being advanced in value
levers.document: Proof that the vehicle was taken abroad (registration, export record); for American goods, proof of U.S. origin and export.
levers.caveat: Repairs and alterations abroad are dutiable on their value (9802.00.40/.50); for Section 232 goods 9802.00.60 is assessed on the full value (note 33(a)). The vehicle must still meet EPA and NHTSA entry rules.

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the base rate and the 25% to 100% extra duties — when the factory price to a trading company is lower than the price you pay
levers.appliesTo: Parts, bicycles, e-bikes and trailers bought through a trading company rather than straight from the maker
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies. AD/CVD deposits follow Commerce's own rules.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when imported vehicles or parts (or vehicles built with them) are exported
levers.appliesTo: Any line; common for parts used in U.S.-built vehicles that are exported
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import, manufacturing and export records.
levers.caveat: AD/CVD deposits are not refundable as drawback, and each Chapter 99 duty's eligibility should be checked first; the 2026 metals proclamations limit drawback on the metals duties.

levers.title: Assemble, hold or re-export in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on vehicles and parts re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until goods leave it for the U.S. market
levers.appliesTo: Any line — used by vehicle assembly plants and parts distributors
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Section 232 vehicles and parts, and deal-rate goods, admitted to a zone must take privileged foreign status (notes 33(i)–(u)), which fixes their duty at admission; the inverted-tariff benefit is lost.

rules.title: Motor vehicles and engines must meet EPA emission standards: the importer files EPA Form 3520-1 (3520-21 for heavy-duty engines) in ACE; a vehicle without an EPA certificate label enters only under an exemption or exclusion (for example by age or for racing) or through an EPA Independent Commercial Importer, and can be held 30 days pending the forms

Vehicles and vehicle equipment must meet the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety, bumper and theft-prevention standards: the importer files the DOT HS-7 declaration; a non-conforming vehicle enters only through a NHTSA Registered Importer for a model NHTSA has found eligible, under bond, or under an exemption (25 or more years old, research, show or display)
Each vehicle carries a 17-character VIN and the manufacturer's certification label; foreign manufacturers of vehicles and equipment designate a U.S. agent for service of process
Snowmobiles, off-highway motorcycles and ATVs are recreational vehicles under EPA's nonroad rules: they need an EPA certificate, and the import rules of 40 CFR part 1068 apply

Bicycles, including low-speed electric bicycles (fully operable pedals, motor under 750 W, under 20 mph on the motor alone), must meet the CPSC bicycle safety standard; low-speed e-bikes are consumer products, not motor vehicles
Carriages and strollers must meet the CPSC safety standard for carriages and strollers

Wheelchairs and mobility scooters are medical devices: mechanical wheelchairs are Class I, powered wheelchairs and motorized three-wheeled vehicles Class II (510(k)); the foreign establishment must be registered and the device listed

Antidumping and countervailing duty cash deposits apply to chassis (China, Mexico, Thailand, Vietnam), steel wheels and steel trailer wheels (China), brake drums (China, Türkiye), golf carts and other low-speed vehicles (China), hand trucks (China) and, provisionally, van-type trailers (China, Mexico, Canada); the importer declares the case number and the exporter's rate, and the order's written scope decides coverage
Country-of-origin marking in English, legible and permanent enough to reach the ultimate purchaser — on the part, bicycle or carton; vehicles carry the origin of the final assembly

Report the Chapter 99 heading with the line: the vehicle heading (9903.94.01, or a deal, quota, USMCA-content or relief heading), the parts heading (9903.94.05/.06 or a deal heading), the truck and bus headings (9903.74.01–.11), or the metals heading; otherwise the Section 301 heading for the country; China list and note 31 headings on top; 9903.03.14 for the Canada Section 338 duty

citations.label: CBP Section 232 FAQs: automobiles and parts

groups.label: Tractors: road tractors for semi-trailers, farm and track-laying tractors
groups.note: Road tractors are trucks for the Section 232 truck duty (25%) and need EPA and DOT entry papers; farm tractors are nonroad equipment (EPA nonroad engine rules) and carry the 15% metals duty.

groups.label: Buses, coaches and vans for 10 or more people
groups.note: Buses pay +10% Section 232 from every country, USMCA included. Electric buses from China add 100%.

groups.label: Cars, SUVs, minivans, EVs, hybrids, ATVs, golf carts and snowmobiles
groups.note: The note 33(b) lines (8703.22–8703.90) pay the Section 232 auto duty; 8703.10 and 8703.21 are outside it and carry the metals duty instead. EPA Form 3520-1 and DOT HS-7 at entry; 25-year-old vehicles are exempt from FMVSS and from the Section 232 duty.

groups.label: Trucks and pickups: light trucks, heavy trucks, dump trucks
groups.note: Light trucks (up to 5 t) pay the auto duty, heavier trucks the truck duty; both at 25%. Cab chassis (8704.22.11) pay a 4% base rate, complete trucks 25%.

groups.label: Special-purpose vehicles: mobile cranes, fire trucks, concrete mixers, wreckers
groups.note: Mobile cranes and drilling derricks: metals duty on mobile equipment; concrete mixers and other special trucks: truck duty; fire trucks: Section 301 only.

groups.label: Chassis fitted with engines
groups.note: Chassis for cars are auto parts; chassis for trucks and buses are trucks or truck parts. Chinese chassis for container trailers are not here but in 8716 (AD/CVD).

groups.label: Vehicle bodies and cabs
groups.note: Car bodies are auto parts, truck and bus bodies truck parts (25%), when used in those vehicles.

groups.label: Auto parts: bumpers, brakes, gearboxes, axles, wheels, radiators, steering, airbags
groups.note: Most lines are on the auto-parts (33(g)) and truck-parts (38(i)) lists: 25% only when the article is such a part. Chinese and Turkish brake drums and Chinese steel wheels carry AD/CVD deposits.

groups.label: Works trucks for factories, warehouses and airports (tugs, tow tractors)
groups.note: Works trucks are on the truck list (25%); their parts pay the truck-parts duty when used in such vehicles.

groups.label: Tanks and armored fighting vehicles
groups.note: Free at base; only the Section 301 duty for the country applies.

groups.label: Motorcycles, scooters, mopeds and e-bikes
groups.note: Motorcycles need EPA and DOT papers; e-bikes that meet the low-speed electric bicycle definition follow the CPSC bicycle rules instead. Canadian motorcycles over 800 cc are banned.

groups.label: Bicycles and other non-motorized cycles
groups.note: CPSC bicycle standard (16 CFR 1512). Chinese bicycles pay 25% List 3 plus 12.5%.

groups.label: Wheelchairs and mobility carriages
groups.note: FDA medical devices; Free at base, Section 301 duty for the country only.

groups.label: Parts of motorcycles, bicycles and wheelchairs
groups.note: Bicycle parts pay Free to 10% at base; no Section 232 duty.

groups.label: Baby carriages, strollers and parts
Trailers, semi-trailers, campers, container chassis, hand trucks and carts
groups.note: Trailers and semi-trailers with lighting must meet FMVSS (DOT HS-7). Most trailers, hand trucks and trailer parts carry the 25% metals duty; chassis, van-type trailers, steel trailer wheels and hand trucks face AD/CVD.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations and the tariff schedule — not legal advice. Whether a vehicle is a passenger vehicle, light truck or MHDV, whether an article is a vehicle part, what share of a vehicle is U.S. content and which AD/CVD case applies depend on the facts of each shipment, and the Section 232 and Section 301 headings change by proclamation and notice; confirm with CBP (a binding ruling under 19 CFR part 177), EPA and NHTSA before importing.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for cars, trucks, auto parts, motorcycles, bicycles and trailers. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Cars pay a 2.5% base rate and pickups 25%, plus the 25% Section 232 automobile duty in force since April 3, 2025: 27.5% for a car from most countries.
The EU, Japan and South Korea pay 15% in total on cars, SUVs and listed parts (a 25% pickup stays 25%); UK cars pay 10% inside a 100,000-vehicle quota.
USMCA cars and trucks from Mexico and Canada pay 25% only on their non-U.S. content once Commerce approves it; USMCA parts pay nothing.
Chinese EVs pay 127.5%: 2.5% + 100% Section 301 + 25% Section 232. Other Chinese cars pay 52.5%.
Listed auto parts pay 25% (from May 3, 2025) only when they are car or light-truck parts; trucks over 5 t and their parts pay 25% and buses 10% since November 1, 2025.
Motorcycles, bicycles, e-bikes and other goods outside Section 232 pay the 2026 Section 301 duty for their country (10%–12.5%; China 25% more). The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026.
Every vehicle needs EPA Form 3520-1 and the DOT HS-7 at entry; a vehicle at least 25 years old is exempt from the U.S. safety standards and from the Section 232 duty.

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 87 cover?
faqs.answer: Chapter 87 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule covers vehicles other than railway rolling stock and their parts: tractors (8701), buses (8702), cars and SUVs (8703), trucks (8704), special-purpose vehicles (8705), chassis (8706), bodies (8707), auto parts (8708), works trucks (8709), armored vehicles (8710), motorcycles and e-bikes (8711), bicycles (8712), wheelchairs (8713), bike and motorcycle parts (8714), strollers (8715) and trailers (8716). It has 402 tariff lines; 253 carry a base duty, from 1.4% to 25%.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on imported cars in 2026, and is it still in effect?
searchedAs: how much is the tariff on cars
are tariffs on cars still in effect
faqs.answer: Yes. Cars, SUVs, minivans and light trucks pay their base rate (2.5% for cars, 25% for pickups) plus a 25% Section 232 duty (9903.94.01) in force since April 3, 2025, new or used: 27.5% for a car from most countries. It was not part of the IEEPA tariffs that ended February 24, 2026. Lower totals: 15% for the EU, Japan and South Korea, 10% for UK cars inside the quota, 25% of the non-U.S. content for USMCA vehicles. Chinese EVs pay 127.5%.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on cars from Japan, Germany and South Korea?
searchedAs: tariff on german cars in us
faqs.answer: Cars and SUVs from Japan (since September 16, 2025), the EU including Germany (since August 1, 2025) and South Korea (since November 1, 2025) pay 15% in total — the 2.5% base rate and the Section 232 duty combined (9903.94.41, 9903.94.51, 9903.94.61): $4,500 on a $30,000 car. Pickups keep their 25% rate. Listed auto parts from these countries also pay 15%. Heavy trucks and buses have no deal rate.

faqs.question: How are cars from Mexico and Canada taxed under USMCA?
searchedAs: tariffs on cars from canada to us
faqs.answer: A car or light truck that qualifies for USMCA pays no base rate and a 25% Section 232 duty only on the value of its non-U.S. content (9903.94.03), once the Secretary of Commerce approves the importer's documentation of U.S. content (parts wholly obtained, produced or substantially transformed in the United States); the U.S. content is entered at 0% under 9903.94.02. A $30,000 car with $12,000 of approved U.S. content pays $4,500. Without an approval it pays 25% of the full value; without a USMCA claim 27.5%. USMCA parts pay nothing. Heavy trucks follow the same content rule; buses pay 10%. Canadian golf carts and vehicles up to 1,000 cc also pay a 50% Section 338 duty.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on cars from the UK?
searchedAs: tariffs on uk cars to us
faqs.answer: UK passenger cars pay 10% (2.5% base + 7.5%, 9903.94.31) within a tariff-rate quota of 100,000 vehicles a year — no more than 25,000 a quarter, plus unused quantity carried forward — and 27.5% once CBP reports the quota filled. UK light trucks have no quota (25% + 25%). Listed UK auto parts pay 10% in total (9903.94.32).

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on Chinese EVs?
faqs.answer: A Chinese electric or plug-in hybrid car pays 127.5%: the 2.5% base rate, 100% under the 2024 Section 301 increase (9903.91.03, since September 27, 2024) and 25% Section 232. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty does not apply to Section 232 vehicles. A $40,000 EV owes $51,000. Gasoline cars and conventional hybrids from China pay 52.5% (25% List 1 instead of 100%). EV batteries shipped separately are in Chapter 85.

faqs.question: Which auto parts pay the Section 232 tariff, and how much?
searchedAs: tariffs on car parts from china
tariffs on car parts from canada to us
faqs.answer: The parts listed in U.S. note 33(g) to Chapter 99 — engines, transmissions, axles, brakes, bodies, chassis and most of heading 8708, plus tires, glass, batteries, lights, wiring sets and seats in other chapters — pay their base rate plus 25% (9903.94.05) since May 3, 2025, but only when they are parts of passenger vehicles or light trucks. Totals: 15% from the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, 10% for listed UK parts, nothing under USMCA, 52.5% for a Chinese part (adds 25% List 3). Truck and bus parts on the note 38(i) list pay 25% since November 1, 2025.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on trucks and buses?
faqs.answer: Since November 1, 2025 medium- and heavy-duty vehicles — road tractors, trucks over 5 t, dumpers, concrete mixers, works trucks — pay their base rate (4% or 25%) plus 25% (9903.74.01), and buses 2% plus 10% (9903.74.02), from every country; there are no EU, Japan or Korea deal rates. USMCA trucks pay 25% of the non-U.S. content; USMCA buses still pay 10%. A $150,000 road tractor from outside North America pays 29%.

faqs.question: What is the chicken tax on pickup trucks?
faqs.answer: The "chicken tax" is the 25% general base rate on light trucks (8704.21, 8704.31, 8704.41, 8704.51; G.V.W. up to 5 t) and on most heavier trucks — ten times the 2.5% rate on cars. Korea's KORUS rate on these trucks is also 25%. Since 2025 the Section 232 duty adds 25% more (50% in total) unless the truck is from the EU, Japan or Korea (15% floor, so the total stays 25%) or qualifies for USMCA (Free base, 25% of the non-U.S. content).

faqs.question: What do I need to import a car into the U.S.?
searchedAs: importing a car to the us
importing a used car to the us
importing a car to usa from uk
importing a car from japan to the us
bringing a car to the us from canada
importing a car to the us from europe
faqs.answer: At entry you file EPA Form 3520-1 (19 CFR 12.73) and the DOT HS-7 declaration (19 CFR 12.80, 49 CFR 591.5), and pay the duty for the car's origin. A car built to U.S. standards carries the EPA label and the FMVSS certification label. A non-conforming car must be brought into compliance by a NHTSA Registered Importer for an eligible model and by an EPA Independent Commercial Importer, unless an exemption applies (for example 25 years or older for NHTSA). Your own U.S. car returning from abroad re-enters duty-free (19 CFR 148.32).

faqs.question: What is the 25-year import rule?
faqs.answer: A motor vehicle at least 25 years old does not have to meet the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards to be imported (49 U.S.C. 30112(b)(9); box 1 of the HS-7, 49 CFR 591.5(i)). For tariffs, a passenger vehicle or light truck made in a year at least 25 years before the year of entry is also exempt from the 25% Section 232 duty (9903.94.04), but it pays the 2026 Section 301 duty: 12.5% in total from Japan, 10% from the EU. EPA emission rules are separate (40 CFR 85.1511).

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on bicycles and e-bikes?
faqs.answer: Bicycles (8712) pay 11%, or 5.5% for light road bikes and certain wheel sizes, plus the 2026 Section 301 duty for the country: 48.5% for a standard Chinese bicycle (adds 25% List 3 and 12.5%), 23.5% from Vietnam, 21% from India, 11% from Taiwan or the EU (their 10% rate replaces only a lower base rate). E-bikes are classified with motorcycles (8711.60, Free): 37.5% from China, 12.5% from Vietnam, 10% from the EU or Taiwan. Neither pays Section 232. Low-speed e-bikes must meet the CPSC bicycle standard.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for cars and car parts?
faqs.answer: Cars and SUVs are in heading 8703, by engine type and size: 8703.22–8703.24 gasoline, 8703.31–8703.33 diesel, 8703.40–8703.70 hybrids, 8703.80 electric (8703.80.00.20 new). Car parts are in 8708: bumpers 8708.10, body parts 8708.29, brakes 8708.30, gearboxes 8708.40, axles 8708.50, wheels 8708.70, shock absorbers 8708.80, radiators 8708.91, exhausts 8708.92, clutches 8708.93, steering 8708.94, airbags 8708.95 and other parts 8708.99. Tires (4011), batteries (8507) and engines (8407–8408) are classified elsewhere.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on motorcycles?
faqs.answer: Motorcycles are Free up to 700 cc and 2.4% above, and are not under Section 232, so they pay the 2026 Section 301 duty for their country: 10% from the EU, 12.5% from Japan, 10% or 12.4% from India, 20%–39.9% from China (7.5% or 25% list duty plus 12.5%). Motorcycles over 800 cc from Canada are banned from importation since September 29, 2026. Motorcycle parts (8714.10) are Free plus the same country duty.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on trailers and chassis?
faqs.answer: Trailers and semi-trailers (8716) are Free at base, but campers, van and platform trailers and container chassis carry the 25% Section 232 metals duty (9903.82.09), and trailer parts 3.1% plus 25%. Chinese trailers add 25% List 3. Chassis from China (188.05% AD, 44.32% CVD), Mexico, Thailand and Vietnam carry AD/CVD deposits, Chinese intermodal chassis pay another 100% from November 10, 2026, and van-type trailers from China, Mexico and Canada are under AD/CVD investigation.
